title: Triggers Are Essential for Changing Habits
author: Admired Leadership
summary: A practical treatment of habit change that locates the critical skill not in willpower but in perception. The premise is that old habits cannot simply be added around — the new behaviour must displace the old one — and the swap happens at a trigger point that will route the person toward one habit or the other. The piece supplies a five-part taxonomy of triggers: location, time, emotional state, people, and preceding action, each with a worked example. It then applies the framework to a leadership habit: a leader who answers questions too quickly and wants instead to seek clarity first should recognise the direct question itself as a preceding-action trigger, and rehearse an alternative response against it. The essay is realistic about the learning curve, conceding that leaders will spot the trigger and still miss the opportunity at first, but argues that sustained attention to the trigger makes substitution progressively easier until the new response becomes automatic.
points: The framing claim is that a new habit cannot be established without killing the old one first, which makes substitution — not addition — the unit of change.
The five-trigger taxonomy (location, time, emotional state, people, preceding action) gives a concrete search procedure for finding what currently cues the unwanted behaviour.
The worked leadership example is answering too fast: the direct question from a team member is itself the trigger, and clarity-seeking is the rehearsed substitute.
The author concedes that early attempts fail even when the trigger is spotted accurately, so the skill being trained is speed of recognition rather than strength of resolve.
quotes: Because old habits are comfortable and resist change, people have a hard time establishing a new habit without killing the old one first.
The process involved with doing so depends heavily on learning to identify the trigger points that signal that the swap should be made.
Once we determine a trigger exists, the ability to substitute the new habit becomes a much easier choice.
Say, for example, a leader would like to eliminate the habit of responding too quickly when asked a question and replace it with a new habit of seeking clarity before answering.
By becoming attuned to direct questions as triggers, the leader can rehearse and prepare themselves to offer a different response.
But by focusing on the trigger and keeping it top of mind, they soon become more skilled at substituting the new behavior.
In the case of establishing a new habit, identifying the trigger and seeing it quickly is the critical skill.
